Deploying with toft

From inside your project. Sends what is on your disk right now. What gets sent, and how the app is chosen, is on From your machine.

The commands

Section titled “The commands”
Command What it does
toft apps List the apps you can reach
toft create Create an app, naming the slug before claiming it
toft link Write the [app] table, validating the slug first
toft deploy Push the working tree
toft redeploy Rebuild from the repository the app names
toft status Is it up, what is it serving, since when
toft logs Run log; --follow to stream, --deploy <id> for a build log
toft events The failure feed
toft restart · toft start · toft stop Lifecycle
toft rollback Back to a previous release
toft job list · run · runs · logs · cancel
toft task list · create · edit · delete · run · runs · logs
toft store ls · put · get · rm
toft deps The packages, advisories and fixed versions behind a refused deploy
toft sdk vendor Vendor the install’s own app SDK into your project
toft api Call any route with the stored credential

--json on every command, for anything you are parsing.

Flags come before positionals.

Two commands worth knowing about

Section titled “Two commands worth knowing about”

toft task create and its verbs. A task is a schedule you can now make from the client, in the same place as the code that answers it:

--path is required by create; --schedule is optional, and a task without one runs only when something asks.

toft api calls any route on the install with the credential you have already stored, so you never handle a token to try something:

The response goes to stdout verbatim. --data takes JSON inline, @file, or @- for stdin. Nothing prints the credential.

A path matching no route on the install is exit 2 and names the path — a typo is a typo, not an authentication problem, which is the one guess that used to send people to check their credentials.

Exit codes are a contract

Section titled “Exit codes are a contract”

Worth internalising for CI: 1 and 3 are different failures. A build that ran and failed is 1. A credential the install rejected is 3. An install you could not reach at all is 4.

toft job run and toft task run wait by default, and the run’s outcome is the exit code — so a failing nightly job fails your pipeline without you parsing anything. A task that was skipped is exit 1: a firing that did not happen is not a success. That holds under --json too: the document prints and the exit code is the run’s.

A locked app is exit 2, not exit 1. Nothing was attempted and failed — you were refused — and the message names who locked it.

A name that does not resolve is exit 2 in every verb that takes one: toft job run <unknown>, toft task run <unknown>, toft link in a directory already linked.

Every refusal is a document too

Section titled “Every refusal is a document too”

Under --json, a refusal is a document on stdout — error, kind, code, exit — as well as a sentence on stderr. So a script never has to parse English to find out what happened, and a person watching still gets a sentence.

Output is one JSON document per line, not one document per invocation: a failed firing prints the run and then the refusal. Read it a line at a time.

A failed deploy carries why in full — the reason key, the whole message, and whatever the reason points at: a tail of the build log, or the dependency findings.

Unattended mode

Section titled “Unattended mode”

toft detects a non-interactive terminal rather than remembering a flag you set once. It will not prompt, and anything that needed a confirmation is refused with exit 2 instead of hanging.

That is why toft rollback in a pipeline needs --yes.

The install’s address is the install’s answer

Section titled “The install’s address is the install’s answer”

toft asks the install where its apps are served, once per invocation, rather than deriving a URL from the one you typed. So a split-origin install, a custom hostname and a reverse proxy all work without configuration on your side.
